reader_answers.answer: The gas-phase oxygen abundance of galaxies, measured on a consistent electron-temperature scale.
reader_answers.rationale: Correctly identifies the measured physical quantity and scale.

reader_answers.answer: Whether galaxies at redshift roughly 9–10 had already reached the oxygen abundance seen in nearby galaxies.
Gravitational lensing can magnify galaxies and bias or distort their inferred stellar masses. Using only unlensed systems avoids that complication.

The figure plots stellar mass horizontally and gas oxygen abundance vertically, together with nearby benchmark relations. All five galaxies lie below those relations, at about one-fifth of the nearby oxygen level—an average shortfall of roughly 0.69 dex.
reader_answers.rationale: Correct axes, point location, intuitive ratio, and dex shortfall.

reader_answers.answer: The conclusion barely changes. A benchmark directly measured at the relevant masses still gives a shortfall of about 0.65 dex.
reader_answers.rationale: Correctly recalls the benchmark-swap robustness result.

reader_answers.answer: A stacked measurement of roughly 1,500 fainter galaxies also falls about 0.5–0.6 dex below the nearby relation. GN-z11 points in the same direction, though with greater uncertainty.
reader_answers.rationale: Correctly identifies the independent stack and acceptable GN-z11 directional cross-check.

reader_answers.answer: The main systematic uncertainty is the debated absolute calibration of temperature-based oxygen abundances, at around 0.1–0.2 dex. The sample of only five galaxies is an additional limitation.
reader_answers.rationale: Correctly distinguishes the abundance-scale systematic from the sample-size limitation.

reader_answers.answer: It does not claim a formal statistical detection or a validated, peer-reviewed conclusion.
reader_answers.rationale: Mandatory non-detection and validation boundary is understood.
